analysis.one_liner: Charges hardrock miners a fee on proceeds to fund cleanup of abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the two-year Congress; it died in a House subcommittee after referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a fund to clean up the thousands of inactive and abandoned gold, silver, and other hardrock mines in the West, many of which leak polluted drainage into streams and pose safety hazards. To pay for it, companies producing hardrock minerals from public and formerly public mining claims would pay a fee of 2% to 5% of their net proceeds, depending on their profit margin. Small operations with under $500,000 in annual gross proceeds would be exempt. The money would go to federal and state reclamation programs prioritizing the most dangerous sites.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of western mining states, whose streams, land, and safety are threatened by abandoned mines; state and federal agencies that currently cannot afford to prioritize cleanup, and which would receive grants from the fund.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated funding source for reclamation and restoration of abandoned surface and deep mines, including sealing mine entries, replanting land to prevent erosion, treating water pollution from mine drainage, and controlling subsidence [S2][S3].

Prioritizes spending on sites posing extreme danger to public health, safety, and property, with 25% of fees spent in the state where the mine is located and 50% distributed based on each state's historic share of production [S3].

Funds the cleanup without general taxpayer appropriations: the fee is charged to the companies whose past and present operations created the legacy of abandoned mines, per the bill's own findings that lack of funding is the main obstacle to cleanup [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies producing from unpatented or patented mining claims would pay 2% to 5% of net proceeds annually; some of that cost could be passed to consumers through metal prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gold, silver, and hardrock mining companies

drawbacks.text: The fee is calculated on net proceeds after numerous deductions (extraction, transport, refining, marketing, depreciation, insurance, and more), giving operators wide room to reduce their taxable base [S3].
The fund could not be used on sites already designated for cleanup under CERCLA (Superfund) or uranium tailings law, so the largest and most contaminated sites would not benefit [S3].
The bill states it would not reduce similar state fees, so producers could face layered state and federal charges [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the industry's argument that a new production fee raises costs in a cyclical, internationally competitive industry; the bill text does not include an economic analysis of that effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cleanup need is large and well documented in the bill's own findings: thousands of abandoned mines threaten public safety and have damaged thousands of stream miles [S3]. The cost falls on a specific industry that historically paid nothing for reclamation under the 1872 General Mining Law. The main design weakness is the net-proceeds fee base, which is heavily discounted and could shrink collections, and the exclusion of Superfund-listed sites, which limits the fund to smaller problems.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Resources Committee, which sent it to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearings, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Representative Mark Udall of Colorado introduced the bill on March 10, 2005, citing thousands of abandoned mines in the West that pose safety hazards and have damaged thousands of stream miles [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Resources on the day of introduction; the committee never reported it, so it never reached the House floor [S1][S5].

Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and the Interior Department was asked for its comments; no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 109th Congress [S5].
The bill drew only one cosponsor in two years [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, which continued producing without paying any federal reclamation fee, while the public remains responsible for cleanup costs at abandoned sites.

for.name: Rep. Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction, referred it to a subcommittee, and never reported it out for a House vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and its sole cosponsor were Democrats, but the bill aimed at western mining states where members of both parties have historically been involved, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining (gold, silver, copper and other hardrock minerals)
industries.note: The bill would charge producers 2% to 5% of net proceeds to finance cleanup of abandoned mines, a cost the industry does not currently bear under the 1872 General Mining Law. Its interest in avoiding the fee runs against the public's interest in having polluted streams and hazardous sites cleaned up at industry rather than taxpayer expense.

industries.industry: States and agencies that bear abandoned-mine cleanup costs
industries.note: State reclamation programs could receive grants and a share of the fund to inventory and reclaim abandoned sites, relieving budgets now stretched thin [S3].
